q: Isolated chloroplasts with the blue dye DCPIP (colourless when reduced) lose their colour in light but not in the dark. What does this show?
options: DCPIP is oxidised by light energy, which releases extra O2 from the chloroplasts
Light-driven electron flow produces reducing power; DCPIP accepts electrons in place of NADP+
The Calvin cycle has used its ATP to reduce DCPIP while it was fixing CO2 in the stroma
The chloroplasts have made glucose in the light, which bleaches the blue dye as it builds up
explanation: This is the Hill reaction. Electrons excited in the photosystems reduce DCPIP (blue → colourless) instead of NADP+. The rate of colour loss measures the rate of light-dependent electron flow. No CO2 is needed, showing that photolysis, O2 release and reduction happen in the light-dependent stage, independently of carbon fixation.
